# Compilers and Kernels {#sec-compilers-kernels}

A framework program is still several contracts away from executable device code.
The compiler must preserve the program's meaning for every input covered by its
guards (runtime checks that an input still satisfies the assumptions the code
was compiled under), while choosing layouts, fusion boundaries, tile shapes,
library calls, and target instructions. The kernel must then honor the promised
shape, stride, dtype, layout, aliasing, mutation, numerical, and device target
semantics. A faster kernel counts as an optimization only when it satisfies all
of those conditions; one that violates any of them implements a different
program.

This chapter follows the execution path introduced in
@sec-frameworks-autodiff. It begins with the cost models that guide fusion and
tiling, uses FlashAttention to show how an algorithm can be redesigned around a
memory hierarchy, and then traces a graph through intermediate representations
to target code. The final sections separate several meanings of portability and
show why kernels generated by language models need a stronger evaluator than
ordinary application code. Quantized arithmetic and its specialized matrix
kernels remain the focus of @sec-quantization-kernels.

## A kernel implements a bounded contract

A logical operator says what a result means. A kernel is one implementation of
that operator for a declared domain. On a GPU, a launch creates a grid of thread
blocks; the device schedules blocks onto streaming multiprocessors, and groups
of lanes execute together as warps or wavefronts. Threads in one block can
cooperate through shared memory and synchronization. Registers belong to
individual threads, while global device memory is visible across the grid
[@nickolls2008cuda; @nvidia2026programming].

Correctness depends on the launch domain as much as on the kernel body. A
contiguous matrix and a transposed view can have the same logical shape but
different strides. Two arguments may alias the same storage. A reduction may
promise a particular accumulation dtype or tie-breaking rule. A random operator
advances state, and an in-place operator changes storage visible elsewhere. A
compiler may specialize a kernel for these facts, but it must either guard them
at runtime or retain a correct general path.

That gives five distinct responsibilities:

| Layer | Input it sees | Contract it must preserve |
|---|---|---|
| Graph capture | Program execution plus guards | The same observable tensor and state effects while the guards hold |
| Tensor intermediate representation (IR) | Operators, shapes, dtypes, effects | Operator semantics and valid transformations |
| Kernel IR | Tiles, address calculations, memory spaces | Complete writes, legal accesses, ordering, and synchronization |
| Target code | Instructions or external library calls | Compatibility with the selected device and runtime |
| Runtime | Buffers, streams, launch order, compile cache | Lifetimes, dependencies, failures, and fallback behavior |

Performance work begins only after those boundaries are explicit.

## Roofline gives an optimistic bound

The roofline model relates arithmetic work to traffic across a chosen memory
boundary [@williams2009roofline]. For one kernel, define

$$
I=F/Q,
$$

where:

- $F$ is the chosen count of floating-point operations for the kernel;
- $Q$ is the number of bytes transferred across the measured boundary, such as
  high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to the chip;
- $I$ is arithmetic intensity in floating-point operations per byte.

Using a compute ceiling and a bandwidth ceiling for the same target and
precision gives the following bound. Here the two terms represent the compute
and traffic ceilings, respectively:

$$
P_{\text{bound}}=\min\left(P_{\max}, B_{\max}I\right),
$$

and therefore the algorithmic lower bound

$$
T\geq
\max\left(\frac{F}{P_{\max}},\frac{Q}{B_{\max}}\right).
$$

where:

- $P_{\text{bound}}$ is the roofline upper bound on throughput;
- $P_{\max}$ is the relevant compute ceiling in floating-point operations per
  second, using the same dtype and instruction path as $F$;
- $B_{\max}$ is the achieved bandwidth ceiling in bytes per second for the
  relevant access pattern, preferably measured rather than copied from a data
  sheet;
- $T$ is execution time in seconds.

Here, the ridge intensity is $I_{\text{ridge}}=P_{\max}/B_{\max}$. Below it, reducing
traffic can raise the bound; above it, reducing arithmetic or using a faster
compute path can. This is a classification and an optimistic limit, not a
runtime prediction. Launch overhead, dependency latency, insufficient
parallelism, instruction mix, cache behavior, uncoalesced access, bank
conflicts, synchronization, and occupancy can all produce a lower ceiling.
Observed performance should therefore use achieved bandwidth and achieved
compute rates from a profiler, not just nominal peaks.

A Transformer profile can contain operators on both sides of the ridge. Ivanov
et al. found both tensor contractions and memory-bound operators to be material
parts of BERT runtime; removing data movement accelerated the measured workload,
but the result did not imply that every transformer or every operator was
bandwidth-bound [@ivanov2021data].

The cell below measures both ceilings on the machine that runs it instead of
copying them from a data sheet. It times a copy, an add, the unfused chain
$y=\max(ax+b,0)$ over an FP32 vector, and square FP32 matrix multiplies from
$n=8$ to 256, and counts the minimum traffic of each, with every operand crossing
memory once. The unfused chain writes two full intermediates and reads them back,
six vector transfers where a fused kernel needs two. The fastest arithmetic rate
and the fastest streaming rate become $P_{\max}$ and $B_{\max}$. The cell asserts
that every measured time respects $T\geq\max(F/P_{\max},Q/B_{\max})$ and prints
how close each kernel comes to its bound. Small matrix multiplies sit far below
both roofs because the fixed cost of a call, which the model does not contain,
dominates their time. The hollow marker is the fused chain's bound: the same
arithmetic over a third of the traffic. It caps what fusion can gain on this
machine and does not predict it. In the browser numpy runs as WebAssembly, where
arithmetic is far slower than in a native build but a plain copy is not, so the
ridge sits far to the left of where a native run of the same cell puts it.
Change the matrix sizes or the dtype and watch the ridge move.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import time
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def best(f, reps=3):  # seconds per call: repeat until a batch outlasts a coarse browser timer,
    ts, n = [], 1        # and keep the fastest batch, since timer noise only ever adds time
    while len(ts) < reps:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(n):
            f()
        dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
        if dt < 0.005:
            n *= 4
        else:
            ts.append(dt / n)
    return min(ts)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.random(2**22, dtype=np.float32)  # 16 MB
a, b, E = np.float32(1.5), np.float32(-0.5), x.nbytes
ops = {  # name: (F operations, Q bytes counted once per operand, measured seconds)
    "copy": (0, 2 * E, best(x.copy)),
    "x + x": (x.size, 2 * E, best(lambda: x + x)),
    "max(ax+b, 0)": (3 * x.size, 6 * E, best(lambda: np.maximum(a * x + b, 0))),  # 3 kernels, 2 intermediates
}
for n in (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256):
    A, B = rng.random((n, n), dtype=np.float32), rng.random((n, n), dtype=np.float32)
    ops[f"matmul {n}"] = (2 * n**3, 3 * n * n * 4, best(lambda: A @ B))

P = max(F / t for F, Q, t in ops.values())  # measured compute ceiling, FLOP/s
Bw = max(Q / t for F, Q, t in ops.values() if F <= Q)  # measured bandwidth from the streaming ops, B/s
for k, (F, Q, t) in ops.items():
    assert t >= 0.9 * max(F / P, Q / Bw), k  # T >= max(F/P, Q/B) holds for every measured kernel

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4))
I = np.logspace(-2, 2, 200)
ax.loglog(I, np.minimum(P, Bw * I) / 1e9, color="0.55", lw=1.5)
ax.set_ylim(P / 1e9 / 100, P / 1e9 * 2)  # at least two decades, whatever this machine measures
for k, (F, Q, t) in ops.items():
    if F:
        ax.plot(F / Q, F / t / 1e9, "o", color="#5b8def")
        ax.annotate(k, (F / Q, F / t / 1e9), fontsize=7, xytext=(5, -8), textcoords="offset points")
F, Q, t = ops["max(ax+b, 0)"]
ax.plot(3 * F / Q, min(P, Bw * 3 * F / Q) / 1e9, "o", mfc="none", color="#ff7a66")
ax.annotate("fused bound", (3 * F / Q, min(P, Bw * 3 * F / Q) / 1e9), fontsize=7, color="#ff7a66",
            xytext=(5, 4), textcoords="offset points")
ax.set_xlabel("arithmetic intensity I (FLOP/byte)"); ax.set_ylabel("attained GFLOP/s")
ax.set_title(f"Measured here: {Bw / 1e9:.1f} GB/s, {P / 1e9:.1f} GFLOP/s, ridge at I = {P / Bw:.2f}", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
print("kernel        % of bound")
for k, (F, Q, t) in ops.items():
    print(f"{k:13s}{100 * max(F / P, Q / Bw) / t:5.0f}")
```

## Fusion is a legality and resource decision

Fusion combines producer-consumer operations so an intermediate need not be
materialized in global memory. It can also remove launches and expose algebraic
simplifications. These gains are real only when the combined kernel remains
legal and fits the target well.

A compiler first has to prove that fusion preserves dependencies and observable
effects. Mutation and alias relationships can make an apparently dead
intermediate visible. Random-number state, host callbacks, collectives, atomics,
and exceptions constrain reordering. Reductions need special care because a new
reduction order can change rounding, NaN propagation, and deterministic
behavior. Even pointwise fusion can introduce fused multiply-add instructions
or reassociation, so mathematical equivalence does not imply bitwise identity.

The cost decision comes next. Fusion lengthens live ranges and can increase
register pressure or shared-memory demand. If values spill to local or global
memory, traffic returns in a more expensive form. A larger kernel can lower
occupancy (the fraction of each multiprocessor's thread capacity that is
resident at once), reduce scheduling freedom, duplicate work, or prevent a call
to a highly tuned library. This is why over-fusion is possible. A useful
compiler estimates bytes removed, launch count, parallelism, and resource use,
then profiles uncertain choices rather than treating fusion as an unconditional
rule [@ansel2024pytorch2].

## Tiling maps work onto finite resources

Tiling chooses a small block of a larger computation and reuses its operands
near the processors. Here, for matrix multiplication, a thread block may load tiles
of $A$ and $B$ from global memory into shared memory, synchronize, perform many
multiply-accumulates into registers, and repeat along the reduction dimension.
Adjacent lanes should make coalesced global-memory accesses so the hardware can
serve them with few transactions.

Each tile shape is a coupled choice. Larger tiles create more reuse but consume more
registers and shared memory. More resident thread blocks can hide latency, yet
maximum occupancy is not itself the goal: a lower-occupancy kernel can still win
if each block does more useful work. Bank conflicts, synchronization frequency,
tail masks, tensor-unit alignment, and the number of pipeline stages also
change the result. When shapes or architectures vary, compilers commonly use
heuristics to narrow the candidates and autotuning to benchmark a finite set of
schedules, where a schedule is the set of loop-order, tiling, and placement
choices that implements one computation [@chen2018tvm; @tillet2019triton;
@triton2026guide].

Autotuning results are conditional artifacts. A winning tile for one shape,
dtype, stride pattern, device, driver, or library version may lose for another.
The cache key must contain every fact on which the choice depends, and a kernel
that mutates its inputs must restore them between trials.

## FlashAttention changes the algorithm around IO

Attention is the Transformer operation that relates positions in a sequence.
Each query position forms a weighted average of value vectors, and the weights
come from how closely its query vector matches every key vector. Scaled
dot-product attention for one head can be written as follows; here the symbols
are defined immediately below:

$$
S=QK^\mathsf{T}/\sqrt{d}+C,
\qquad
P_{ij}=\frac{\exp(S_{ij}-m_i)}{\ell_i},
\qquad
O=PV,
$$

with

$$
m_i=\max_{1\leq j\leq N}S_{ij},
\qquad
\ell_i=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(S_{ij}-m_i).
$$

where:

- $Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}$ are the query and key matrices;
- $V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_v}$ is the value matrix;
- $N$ is sequence length, $d$ is query/key head width, and $d_v$ is value
  width;
- $C\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\})^{N\times N}$ is an additive bias or mask,
  where $-\infty$ disallows a key;
- $S$ is the scaled score matrix, $m_i$ is the maximum of query row $i$, and
  $\ell_i>0$ is its normalizer;
- $P$ is the row-wise softmax matrix, in which each row of exponentiated scores
  is normalized to sum to one;
- $O$ is the attention output, and $\mathsf{T}$ denotes transpose;
- every query row is assumed to have at least one allowed key.

A direct implementation may materialize the complete $N\times N$ score and
probability matrices in HBM. FlashAttention instead processes a query row or
query tile against a sequence of key-value blocks, retaining only tiles and
running statistics in fast memory [@milakov2018online;
@dao2022flashattention]. Here, for one fixed query row $i$, initialize
$m_0=-\infty$, $\ell_0=0$, and $o_0=0\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$. For key-value block
$\mathcal{B}_t$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_t &= \max_{j\in\mathcal{B}_t} S_{ij},\\
m_t &= \max(m_{t-1},b_t),\\
\alpha_t &= \exp(m_{t-1}-m_t),\\
\ell_t &=
\alpha_t\ell_{t-1}
+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}_t}\exp(S_{ij}-m_t),\\
o_t &=
\alpha_t o_{t-1}
+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}_t}\exp(S_{ij}-m_t)v_j.
\end{aligned}
$$

After $T$ blocks,

$$
O_i=o_T/\ell_T.
$$

where:

- $\mathcal{B}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{B}_T$ partition the allowed key indices and
  $t$ is the block index;
- $b_t$ is the maximum score in the current key-value block;
- $m_t$ is the running maximum and $\alpha_t$ rescales earlier contributions
  when that maximum changes;
- $\ell_t$ is the running normalizer;
- $o_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$ is the running value-weighted numerator;
- $v_j$ is row $j$ of $V$, and $O_i$ is output row $i$.

In exact arithmetic, the recurrence maintains the same numerator and
denominator as the full softmax. “Exact attention” refers to that mathematical
function, not bitwise identity: tiling changes floating-point evaluation order.
The algorithm still performs quadratic attention arithmetic. Its gain is that
it does not materialize the complete quadratic intermediates in HBM, and its
backward pass can recompute local score and probability tiles instead of saving
them.

```{figure}
//| figure: flash-attention
//| label: fig-compilers-kernels-flashattention
//| fig-cap: "FlashAttention's forward pass over an illustrative sequence: $Q$, $K$, and $V$ are seeded random draws with $d=d_v=4$, and both the recurrence and the reference softmax run in FP32. Each query tile stays on chip while the key-value blocks $\mathcal{B}_t$ stream through; only the current $S$ tile holds values, shaded by $\exp(S_{ij}-m_t)$. The tiles run one after another here and in parallel on a GPU. For the chosen row $i$, the strips show its scores against the running maximum $m_t$ and the weights $\exp(S_{ij}-m_t)$ of the keys seen so far, with dashed outlines at the heights they had before the current block's $\alpha_t$ rescaled them. The readout evaluates each term of the recurrence and compares $o_t/\ell_t$ with ordinary softmax over the same keys, within a tolerance of $2Nu\max|v|$ for the FP32 unit roundoff $u=2^{-24}$. With rescaling turned off, earlier blocks stay in the frame of their own maximum, the dashed outlines mark the heights they should have, and the output no longer matches. HBM traffic is minimum algorithmic traffic with 2-byte elements: the naive kernel writes $S$ and $P$ and reads them back, while the tiled kernel rereads $K$ and $V$ once per query tile, so a taller tile moves fewer bytes and needs more on-chip memory. Under the causal mask, blocks that lie entirely after a tile's last row are skipped."
```

In the two-level memory model used by the original paper, the forward algorithm
requires

$$
H_{\text{FA}}=\Theta\left(\frac{N^2d^2}{M}\right)
$$

slow-memory word transfers for $d\leq M\leq Nd$, where $H_{\text{FA}}$ is the
transfer count and $M$ is fast-memory capacity in scalar words. This is an IO
statement, not a FLOP or byte count; bytes also depend on the stored dtype.
Later work proved a matching pointwise lower bound, within constant factors,
for $M\geq d^2$ and found a different regime below that threshold
[@saha2024attentionio]. It is therefore incorrect to call the original
algorithm optimal for every possible SRAM size.

FlashAttention-2 improved work partitioning and reduced non-matrix operations
on the A100 configurations reported in its paper
[@dao2023flashattention2]. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper-specific asynchronous
copy and matrix instructions in its reported H100 results
[@shah2024flashattention3]. Together they show that algorithmic IO savings can
transfer across targets, while the best schedule often remains target-specific.

## Lowering preserves meaning while adding decisions

Compilers use multiple intermediate representations because no single level is
ideal for every decision. A high-level tensor IR can still express
broadcasting, reductions, effects, and symbolic dimensions from the captured
graph. A lower kernel IR
can express tiles, address calculations, memory spaces, barriers, and target
instructions. Progressive lowering makes each new choice explicit while
retaining the information needed to check it. Halide established the influential
separation between an algorithm and its schedule; TVM added tensor-graph
optimization and measurement-guided schedule search; MLIR provides reusable
infrastructure for defining and composing such IR levels
[@ragankelley2013halide; @chen2018tvm; @lattner2021mlir].

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compilers-kernels-lowering
//| fig-cap: "A generic lowering pipeline. Portable tensor semantics narrow into target-specific schedules and artifacts; generated kernels and external library calls are both valid leaves."
digraph lowering {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.28;
  ranksep=0.32;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280", penwidth=1.0];

  source [label="program + runtime facts"];
  capture [label="capture / export\nguards + effects"];
  tensor [label="tensor IR\ndecomposition + shapes"];
  optimize [label="graph optimization\nfusion + layout + buffer planning"];
  select [label="kernel IR or library call\ntiling + schedule + autotuning"];
  nvidia [label="NVIDIA target\nPTX / cubin"];
  amd [label="AMD target\nLLVM / HSACO"];
  tpu [label="TPU target\nbackend executable"];
  runtime [label="device runtime\nbuffers + streams + launches"];

  source -> capture -> tensor -> optimize -> select;
  select -> nvidia;
  select -> amd;
  select -> tpu;
  nvidia -> runtime;
  amd -> runtime;
  tpu -> runtime;
}
```

The diagram is deliberately generic. A compiler may preserve a high-level
operation as a library call rather than generate a kernel. Matrix
multiplication, convolution, and collectives often take this path because a
vendor or framework library already contains many target-specific algorithms.
Other regions lower to a kernel IR, where fusion, layout, and resource choices
become explicit.

### PyTorch's guarded path

For `torch.compile`, TorchDynamo captures guarded FX graph segments from Python
execution. Training adds AOTAutograd, which captures and partitions forward and
backward graphs and applies decompositions and functionalization, which
rewrites in-place mutation as pure operations. TorchInductor then schedules
loop-level IR and can emit Triton GPU kernels, C++ CPU kernels, template
kernels, or calls to external operators [@ansel2024pytorch2;
@pytorch2026compiler]. A graph break returns unsupported work to eager
execution, where Python runs operators one at a time. A guard failure can
select another compile cache entry,
trigger recompilation, or force a more general path.

Dynamic shapes do not remove specialization. Symbolic dimensions and guards
allow some compiled regions to cover many inputs, but values, ranks, strides,
and target features may still require distinct code. Compile latency, guard
failure, graph breaks, and cache growth are therefore part of the production
cost model.

### JAX and OpenXLA

JAX traces a specialized Python function into jaxpr, its intermediate
representation. Lowering converts the
program through StableHLO into XLA's optimization and code-generation pipeline.
XLA performs target-dependent fusion, layout assignment, buffer planning,
collective handling, and kernel or library selection before a target executable
is loaded through the runtime [@frostig2018jax; @openxla2026stablehlo;
@openxla2026emitters].

StableHLO defines portable tensor semantics and a compatibility window for
portable artifacts. It does not freeze a physical layout, schedule, numerical
accuracy across every consumer, or performance. Those decisions belong to the
consumer and target. JAX also specializes on facts such as shape, dtype, and
static arguments, so its compile cache needs the same operational attention as
any other staged system.

## Layout and autotuning are part of compilation

Logical shape does not determine physical layout. A compiler may choose which
dimension is contiguous, add padding or tiling, place buffers in different
memory spaces, or distribute tile elements across lanes and registers. Some
transposes are metadata changes; others move the entire tensor. Library calls
and matrix instructions impose layout constraints, and converting between two
otherwise valid layouts can erase the gain from a fast kernel.

Schedule selection has the same conditional nature. Triton raises the
programmer's unit of work from a scalar thread to a blocked program, while its
compiler handles tasks such as coalescing, vectorization, shared-memory
allocation, and instruction selection [@tillet2019triton;
@triton2026guide]. The author still chooses the grid, masks, tile sizes, number
of warps or stages, and sometimes target-specific mechanisms. TVM-style learned
cost models and empirical autotuning search over choices; they do not make one
schedule universally optimal.

## Portability names five separate claims

Claims about a “portable kernel” need a named boundary:

| Portability claim | What it means | What it does not guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Source portability | One source language can be accepted by several backends | Equal feature coverage or identical generated code |
| Semantic portability | Backends implement the declared operator behavior | Bitwise-identical floating-point results |
| Artifact portability | A serialized IR or binary loads in its promised compatibility window | Portability outside that artifact ecosystem |
| Performance portability | One implementation remains efficient across targets | Implied by source or semantic portability |
| Operational portability | Tooling, deployment, observability, and fallback work on each target | Implied by a successful kernel launch |

PTX is an NVIDIA virtual instruction set, not a universal GPU IR. CUDA device
code may be shipped as PTX, target-specific cubin, or a fat binary containing
several images. PTX can be assembled ahead of time or JIT-compiled by the
driver; cubin compatibility is narrower [@nvidia2026nvcc]. An AMD backend may
instead lower through AMD LLVM to an HSACO artifact, while a TPU backend emits
its own executable. These branches can share high-level tensor semantics without
sharing a final schedule or binary.

The same distinction applies to Triton. Its blocked programming model can
reduce source duplication across supported targets, but backend coverage,
available instructions, layout choices, and tuned configurations still differ.
A target-specific schedule is often needed for performance portability, and
that schedule must be revalidated as hardware and compilers change.

## The ecosystem is part of the target

CUDA began as a programming and execution model, but applications depend on a
larger contract: the driver and runtime; compiler and artifact formats; math and
communication libraries; profiler and debugger behavior; framework
integration; and the accumulated tests and operational knowledge around them
[@nickolls2008cuda; @chetlur2014cudnn]. Alternative targets have corresponding
stacks. Comparing only a kernel language or a peak arithmetic rate therefore
misses much of the switching cost.

Library contracts include supported dtypes and layouts, workspace limits,
algorithm selection, determinism, stream semantics, collective ordering, ABI
compatibility, and target generations.
Moving a workload means finding equivalent behavior for every relied-upon
contract, then validating numerical results and performance on the actual shape
distribution. Source translation can reduce labor, but it does not discharge
that verification.

This is also a research constraint. The “hardware lottery” describes how ideas
that map well to available hardware and software receive cheaper, faster
experiments [@hooker2021hardware]. A new model architecture may look weak
because it lacks a fused scan, sparse operation, or layout-aware compiler path,
not because its mathematical idea is weak. Kernel availability therefore affects
which model designs can be evaluated credibly.

## Generated kernels need a hostile evaluator

KernelBench made the evaluation of model-generated kernels concrete with 250
PyTorch workloads and a metric that requires both correctness and speed
[@ouyang2025kernelbench]. For task set $\mathcal{D}$, one version of that metric
can be written

$$
\operatorname{fast}_p
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[
\operatorname{correct}(k_i)
\land
t(k_i)<\frac{t(b_i)}{p}
\right].
$$

where:

- $\mathcal{D}$ is the benchmark task set and $|\mathcal{D}|$ its size;
- $k_i$ is the generated kernel for task $i$ and $b_i$ is its baseline;
- $t(\cdot)$ is synchronized execution time under the benchmark protocol;
- $p>0$ is the required speedup threshold;
- $\operatorname{correct}(k_i)$ is the benchmark's semantic verdict;
- $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise.

Execution and profiling feedback can improve results, and training a model to
revise its kernel over multiple rounds of such feedback has shown gains on
fixed benchmark splits [@baronio2025kevin]. Those results do
not establish general kernel reliability. A kernel can pass a few shapes while
writing only part of its output, rely on narrow input distributions, mutate an
input, call the reference path, or exploit allocator and synchronization state.
Follow-up audits have demonstrated that broader hidden distributions and
stricter baselines can reverse apparent wins
[@kernelbenchverified2026]. This is the same evaluator problem examined in
@sec-verifiers-process-supervision, now with asynchronous hardware and mutable
memory added.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compilers-kernels-validation
//| fig-cap: "A generated kernel is accepted only after independent semantic, compiler, and performance gates. Failures return to the generator or a known fallback, never directly to production."
digraph validation {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.32;
  ranksep=0.32;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8, fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  generator [label="kernel generator\nmodel or search"];
  candidate [label="candidate kernel"];
  compile [label="compiler gate\nbuild + sanitizer"];
  semantic [label="semantic gate\nhidden randomized tests"];
  performance [label="performance gate\nsynchronized representative trials"];
  accept [label="versioned artifact\ncanary + rollback", color="#3b82f6",
          fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];
  reject [label="reject or fallback"];

  // One group keeps the accept path in a straight column; the fail and
  // feedback edges run beside it.
  generator [group=main]; candidate [group=main]; compile [group=main];
  semantic [group=main]; performance [group=main]; accept [group=main];

  generator -> candidate -> compile -> semantic -> performance -> accept;
  compile -> reject [label="fail"];
  semantic -> reject [label="fail"];
  performance -> reject [label="fail"];
  reject -> generator [label="feedback", style=dashed, constraint=false];
}
```

A production evaluator should cover at least:

1. **Contract surface.** Freeze supported ranks, shapes, dtype and math mode,
   device architecture, alignment, layout, aliasing, mutation, workspace,
   stream, error, and determinism behavior.
2. **Hidden semantics.** Use fresh random inputs and outputs, boundary shapes,
   zero and odd sizes, broadcast cases, noncontiguous strides, misalignment,
   cancellation, ties, signed zeros, NaN and infinity where supported, and
   independent tolerances derived from dtype and reduction length.
3. **Memory and concurrency.** Detect out-of-bounds access, uninitialized data,
   incomplete writes, races, bad synchronization, illegal aliasing, and failures
   under concurrent streams, graph replay, and varied allocator histories.
4. **Harness integrity.** Isolate the candidate; prevent reference calls,
   monkey-patching, hidden fallback, network or file access, and reuse of
   reference allocation state. Perturb every input so the output must depend on
   it.
5. **Measurement.** Separate compile time, autotuning, cold-start latency,
   kernel-only time, and end-to-end time. Use warm-up, device synchronization,
   randomized paired order, many repetitions, and a median plus useful
   quantiles or confidence intervals.
6. **Representative comparison.** Match dtype, fast-math settings, layout,
   workspace, graph mode, and hardware. Compare with a production baseline, not
   only an eager reference, over the real workload distribution.

## Operating the compiler-kernel boundary

A reliable release process treats the generated artifact and its assumptions as
one unit:

1. Record the graph or operator schema, guards, effect and alias model,
   numerical tolerance, and fallback.
2. Pin the target architecture, driver, runtime, math libraries, compiler,
   toolchain version, flags, and autotuning state.
3. Build a semantic gate covering eager-versus-compiled outputs, gradients when
   relevant, edge shapes, strides, dtypes, mutation, and concurrency.
4. Build a compiler gate covering graph breaks, guard failures, recompilations,
   compile cache growth, sanitizer findings, and target-code generation.
5. Build a performance gate over the representative workload distribution,
   measuring launch count, achieved bandwidth or compute, occupancy, registers,
   shared memory, spills, workspace, and peak memory.
6. Report cold-start compilation and autotuning separately from warm execution.
7. Canary the artifact with automatic rollback to the known fallback on
   numerical, compiler, or latency regression.
8. Re-run the gates whenever the graph, target, driver, library, compiler, or
   workload distribution changes.

## Lower-layer constraint

The compiler cannot recover information that the framework discarded, prove
aliasing facts the program did not expose, or make an unsupported target
instruction exist. Conversely, a kernel can be locally fast and still lose
end-to-end because its layout forces a transpose, its workspace raises memory
pressure, its compile cache fragments on dynamic shapes, or its launch breaks a
larger fusion region. Compiler and kernel performance must therefore be
measured in the graph and service that consume them, against the bandwidth,
memory, and interconnect limits from @sec-accelerators-networking.

The next chapter, @sec-orchestration-data-infra, moves up one layer, from
producing executable work to keeping a long-running training system supplied,
observable, and recoverable.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Compilers already generate useful kernels. The unsettled question is how much
target-specific information can remain behind a portable interface without a
significant loss of performance. High-level IRs
and blocked kernel languages improve source and semantic portability. New
device instructions, layout rules, library contracts, and asynchronous
pipelines keep creating target-specific scheduling work. Generated-kernel
systems may reduce that labor, but their gains remain conditional on the
evaluator, baseline, shape distribution, hardware, and search budget. A
testable form of the claim therefore names a workload and a contract and asks
whether the toolchain preserves semantics and beats the best maintained
fallback after compile and operating costs are included.
:::
